name: Femi Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I run my week like a small business. I'm doing software engineering, and I share a rented flat with my older cousin Tariq and a friend from school, which keeps rent low. Lectures are Monday to Wednesday. Thursday to Saturday I work at a phone repair and IT help shop in the market, fixing screens and setting up laptops for older customers. On Fridays I go to the mosque with Tariq, and afterwards we eat with the family.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where did the business-minded part come from?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle. He started with one market stall and now has three shops, and he always says nobody hands you anything. I use AI tools all day, for code, for writing quotes for the shop, even for working out what to charge. I'm picking up skills quickly, and I'd like to run a business of my own by the time I'm thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool but people exaggerate, and I wouldn't be surprised. I'd tell the lads at the shop that nothing replaces someone who shows up on time and fixes the problem. I'd say that the people who succeed are the ones who work hard and use what's available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine about my skills, but the money side is tight. My loan covers fees and my shop wages cover rent, and my savings are less than a month. If the shop owner cut my hours or the market had a quiet season, I'd feel it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my course and the shop, but I'd start a small side business of my own, like setting up smart-home gadgets for older people. I'd take more hours when the owner offers them, and I'd save a third of each wage. I'd also keep up with the new tools, because they save me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Motivated, I'd say. A plain world suits me, because hard work gets rewarded there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you worry about in a plain world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cash flow, honestly. When the market is quiet, I make half as much in a week, and there's no safety net apart from Tariq and my own pocket. I can plan for a bad week, but a bad month would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of the shop work uses AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quotes and the customer emails, mostly. I also ask it to explain odd faults on phones I haven't seen before. It's quicker than the manuals, though the owner still checks anything I give a customer.

say: I'd say it's a good **tool** but people exaggerate.
I'd tell the lads at the shop that people who show up and **work hard** do well.
think: I'm fine about my skills, but **money** is tight and my savings are under a month.
A quiet **market season** or cut hours would be felt quickly.
do: Start a small **side business** setting up smart-home gadgets for older people.
feel: **Motivated**: a plain world suits me because hard work gets rewarded.
S0.quote: When the market is quiet, I make half as much in a week, and there's no safety net apart from Tariq and my own pocket
fieldNote: His worry is **cash flow** in quiet market weeks, not AI.
He uses AI for **quotes**, emails and odd phone faults, with the owner checking.
He wants a **side business** immediately, which fits his adaptive side.

steps.text: Offer smart-home set-up to older customers on Saturdays
Save a third of every shop wage
Use AI to speed up quotes and fault-finding at the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity if you're quick, and a problem if you're not. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and spot gaps that the tools leave. I'd say the government should stay out of the way, but make sure people have a decent chance to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it as a chance. The card says coding is first in line, and that is my course, so I'd have to be careful. But I'm already ahead with the tools, and I'd rather build something than wait to be hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to start a small software service, maybe a booking tool for market stall owners, since I know their problems. I'd use AI to build it faster than I could alone, and aim for ten paying customers by summer. I'd also join the university's start-up society, because I'd meet people who've done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumped, and a bit under pressure. If I'm honest, I like being ahead of the curve, but I also know the ones who are ahead are the first people watched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What problem would the tool solve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stall owners lose money because they forget to restock and they lose customers to no-shows on repairs. A simple booking and reminder tool for market stalls costs almost nothing to build now, and a stall owner will pay for something that stops no-shows. I've watched it happen at our shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your uncle say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say 'good, now sell it'. He's never impressed by an idea, only by a customer. I'd probably pitch it at him first and see if he'd use it at the shops.

say: I'd say it's a big **opportunity** if you're quick, and a problem if you're not.
I'd say government should stay out of the way but fund **retraining**.
think: I see it as a **chance**, though coding is first in line and that's my course.
I'd rather **build** something than wait to be hired.
do: Start a small **booking tool** for market stall owners.
Use AI to build it faster and aim for ten **paying customers**.
feel: **Pumped**, with some pressure, since being ahead means being watched.
S1.quote: A simple booking and reminder tool for market stalls costs almost nothing to build now, and a stall owner will pay for something that stops no-shows
fieldNote: He turns the card into a **product** idea drawn from his shop work.
He judges ideas by **customers**, just as his uncle does.
The risk he names is **being watched** while ahead.

steps.text: Build a booking and reminder tool for market stalls
Get ten paying stall owners by next summer
Join the start-up society and find a mentor
Use AI to speed up coding on the tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast for anyone to get a grip on it, and the ones who are prepared will do best. I'd tell my cousin and friends that we have to think like owners, not employees, because jobs might not be there. I'd say that the government must not make it harder for people to start something, and also give a short-term safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the ground move. Software engineering, the exact course I'm on, is where the change hits first. I'd be maybe a year in, with loans, and the junior job I want is done by AI for a tenth of the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on a business that doesn't depend on a hiring manager. I'd focus on the shop and the side business, selling services that need a person on site, because robots for hands-on work arrive about three years later. I'd use AI to run as lean as I could, and I'd bring in Tariq as a partner. I'd also stop spending on anything but rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Scared too, but more in my chest than my stomach. I'd feel I had to move now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not worried about not working, I'm worried about doing the right work. I'd tell my uncle that I want to build our own thing so I'm not begging anyone for a junior job that won't exist. He'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the business doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd fall back on the repair work, which is physical, and maybe family help for a short while. I wouldn't be proud about it. I've got a cousin and an uncle, and that's a safety net, even if I don't like using it.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** to get a grip on, and the prepared will do best.
I'd say we should think like **owners**, not employees.
think: I'd feel the **ground move**: software engineering is where the change hits first.
The junior job I want could be done by AI for a **tenth** of the cost.
do: Go all in on a **business** that doesn't depend on a hiring manager.
Sell **on-site services**, since robots for hands-on work arrive about three years later.
Bring **Tariq** in as a partner and stop spending on anything but rent and food.
feel: **Wired** and scared, in my chest more than my stomach.
S2.quote: I'd tell my uncle that I want to build our own thing so I'm not begging anyone for a junior job that won't exist
fieldNote: His response is to become an **owner**, not wait for a job.
He accepts the family as a **safety net**, though reluctantly.
He sees the **on-site** repair work as lasting longer than software.

steps.text: Launch the stall booking tool and on-site repair services
Put the degree on hold if the business needs full time
Cut spending to rent and food only
Ask uncle to pilot the tool in his three shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good window, and the people who use it will come out ahead. I'd tell friends that we should learn the tools and also learn how to sell, because that's what stays valuable. I'd say that the rules should stay light, and that anyone who works hard should have a fair chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about it. I'd be 23, with a degree, some customers, and hopefully a small business running. The loan is the one weight, but five years is enough to pay a chunk off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and grow my side business through the years, adding a service each year. I'd take a placement at a start-up to learn how others do it. I'd also invest the profits back into the business, and save to pay off my loan early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and focused. Five years feels like having a fair race and a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the stall booking tool with ten customers. I'd rather spend the first year proving that I can get ten stall owners to pay me than waiting to find out if a company will hire me. It's a better test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to go straight to cash. I'd drop the placement and push the business harder, with no time to build slowly. With five, I get to grow it, which I prefer.

say: I'd say five years is a **good window**, and users of it will come out ahead.
I'd say we should learn the tools and also learn how to **sell**.
think: I'd feel good: a degree, some **customers** and a small business by 23.
The **loan** is the one weight, but five years can cut it down.
do: Finish the degree and add a **service** to the side business each year.
Take a **start-up** placement to learn how others do it.
Reinvest **profits** and pay the loan early.
feel: **Excited** and focused, like a fair race with a head start.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend the first year proving that I can get ten stall owners to pay me than waiting to find out if a company will hire me
fieldNote: Five years lets him **grow** the business slowly instead of chasing cash.
He wants to prove he can get ten **paying customers** in year one.
He keeps the **loan** as his one admitted weight.

steps.text: Add one new service to the side business each year
Take a placement at a start-up in second year
Put profits back into the business tools
Pay the student loan down early from profits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and it's a great window to build something. I'd tell friends to build skills and a business, and not rely on employers. I'd say that people should look after their families first, then their communities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly calm and keen. By 28 I'd have a degree, experience and maybe a company. The part I'd think about is my uncle, who would be near sixty, and the older shopkeepers in the market, who might not adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, grow the business into a proper firm, and hire one or two people from the community. I'd keep up with the tools, trying each new one in the first week it comes out. And I'd help my uncle bring his shops into the new world, because family should go forward together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confident, with a sense of responsibility. Ten years is long enough to build, and I'd rather be the one who builds it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hire first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone from the market who's good with people, not just computers. I'd hire a young person from our own market, because I know how hard it is to get a first job and I'd like to give one. It's how my uncle started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you from getting complacent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family and my faith. They keep me honest. And a yearly review of the business, where I ask what I'd do differently.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, a great window to build something.
I'd tell friends to build skills and a business, not rely on **employers**.
think: I'd be fairly **calm** and keen: a degree, experience and maybe a company by 28.
I'd think about my **uncle** and older shopkeepers who might not adapt.
do: Finish the degree and grow the business into a proper **firm**.
Hire one or two people from the **community**.
Help my uncle bring his **shops** into the new world.
feel: **Confident**, with a sense of responsibility to build.
S4.quote: I'd hire a young person from our own market, because I know how hard it is to get a first job and I'd like to give one
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **calm**, with growth plans centred on community hiring.
He worries about **older shopkeepers** who might not adapt.
His **family and faith** keep him from complacency.

steps.text: Grow the side business into a registered firm
Hire a young person from the market as a first employee
Set up AI ordering and booking in my uncle's shops

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it gives me no time to build a base, and I'm still in debt. What would help is a quick safety net, easy rules for starting a business, and access to cheap loans for people with ideas.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think being adaptive means being fearless. I use every tool and I take risks, but I'm still in debt and I still check my account every night before I sleep. I'm just choosing to move.

headlineQuote: I use every tool and I take risks, but I'm still in debt and I still check my account every night before I sleep
portrait: Femi is an **18-year-old** software engineering first-year sharing a flat with his cousin Tariq.
He is traditional on family and faith, favours free markets, and uses AI tools every day.
He works at a phone repair and IT help shop and wants his own **business** by thirty.
His worry is cash flow and loan debt, and he checks his account every night.
His mood runs from uneasy to anxious at two years, and calm with ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most, since it leaves no time to build a base while in debt.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a quick **safety net**, easy rules for starting up and cheap loans for people with ideas.
